loadFactor.title: Passenger load factor
loadFactor.content:
Passenger load factor is Revenue Passenger Km (RPK) divided by Available Seat Km (ASK) -- the percentage of seat capacity actually sold and flown. Reported separately for the full-service SIA Group and for Scoot, the low-cost subsidiary.

For Singapore Airlines Limited: both lines collapsed to single digits in FY2021-FY2022 (COVID border closures) and have since recovered above pre-pandemic levels; Scoot typically runs a higher load factor than the Group average as a budget carrier.

What to watch:

  • Load factor falling even as ASK (capacity) grows -- a sign of overcapacity or weakening demand
  • Scoot vs Group gap narrowing or widening, which signals shifting demand mix between premium and budget travel

capacityTraffic.title: Capacity (ASK) and traffic (RPK)
capacityTraffic.content:
ASK (Available Seat Km) is total seats flown multiplied by distance -- the capacity SIA put into the market. RPK (Revenue Passenger Km) is the same calculation for seats actually sold -- the capacity that generated revenue. The gap between the two bars is unsold capacity.

For Singapore Airlines Limited: both collapsed by roughly 85% in FY2021 as the fleet was grounded, then rebuilt through FY2022-FY2024 as routes reopened; FY2026 capacity now exceeds the FY2020 pre-pandemic peak.

What to watch:

  • RPK growing faster than ASK (load factor improving) versus the reverse
  • Capacity growth outpacing the load factor and yield trends below -- more seats does not help if they fly empty or cheap

unitEconomics.title: Unit economics: yield, RASK, CASK
unitEconomics.content:
Passenger yield is passenger revenue per RPK (SGD cents) -- the average fare paid per km flown. RASK is total revenue per ASK -- yield blended with load factor. CASK is operating cost per ASK -- the cost of supplying a seat-km. RASK above CASK means the flying is operationally profitable before financing and tax.

For Singapore Airlines Limited: CASK spiked in FY2021-FY2022 as costs stayed semi-fixed while ASK collapsed, then eased back toward 9 SGD cents as capacity normalised; the RASK-CASK spread is the operating-margin story in unit terms.

What to watch:

  • CASK rising faster than RASK (fuel, staff or airport-charge inflation outpacing pricing power)
  • Yield trending down while load factor rises -- capacity being sold at a discount rather than at a premium

cargo.title: Cargo yield and load factor
cargo.content:
Cargo yield is cargo revenue per cargo tonne-km (CTK, SGD cents) -- the price SIA Cargo charges per unit of belly and freighter capacity. Cargo load factor is the percentage of cargo capacity actually sold.

For Singapore Airlines Limited: cargo yield spiked through FY2021-FY2022 when air-freight rates surged on pandemic supply-chain disruption and a smaller passenger-belly fleet, then eased as passenger capacity (and belly-hold space) returned and freight rates normalised.

What to watch:

  • Cargo yield reverting further toward pre-pandemic levels as global air-freight capacity recovers
  • Cargo load factor falling as passenger belly capacity returns -- more capacity chasing similar freight volumes

fleet.title: Fleet size
fleet.content:
Total group fleet is the combined year-end aircraft count across SIA, SilkAir/Scoot and cargo operations; SIA mainline passenger fleet is the full-service passenger-aircraft subset.

For Singapore Airlines Limited: fleet size is the capacity commitment behind the ASK trend above -- it moves slowly (aircraft orders and leases run years ahead) while load factor and yield respond to demand within a year.

What to watch:

  • Fleet growth outpacing RPK growth -- capacity added ahead of demonstrated demand
  • Widebody/narrowbody and SIA/Scoot mix shifts disclosed in the annual report, not visible in the aggregate count alone

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Singapore Airlines Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Singapore Airlines Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Singapore Airlines Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Singapore Airlines Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Singapore Airlines Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Singapore Airlines Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Singapore Airlines Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Singapore Airlines Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Singapore Airlines Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
